title: The Whisper in the Well
tagline: Some voices should never be answered after Maghrib.
author: Shadow Tales

chapters.title: Chapter I — The Courtyard
chapters.summary: You return to your grandmother's abandoned house. Something in the courtyard knows your name.

chapters.title: Chapter II — What Answers Back
chapters.summary: Dawn does not end it. The village remembers what your family buried.

paragraphs: The taxi leaves before you finish paying. Its red tail-lights shrink down the dirt road and the dark closes behind it like a door.
Your grandmother's house stands exactly as she left it: shutters hanging, jasmine gone black on the walls, the old well squatting in the courtyard under its stone lid.
You were told three things as a child. Never whistle at night. Never leave a bowl of water uncovered. And never — never — answer when you are called by name after Maghrib.
The sky is the colour of a bruise. The adhan from the far mosque has just ended.
Somewhere beneath your feet, a woman begins to hum.
The hum stops. A voice rises from under the floorboards — soft, warm, unmistakably your mother's. She died when you were six.
"Habibi… come down. It is so cold here. I have been waiting so long."
Your phone has no signal. The gate chain behind you rattles, though there is no wind.
The cellar door opens without a sound. Stairs of wet stone descend into air that smells of rust and old incense.
At the bottom, the well-shaft pierces the ceiling and continues into the floor — a throat of black bricks. Scratched into them, hundreds of tiny marks. Names.
On a ledge sits a sealed letter in your grandmother's handwriting, and a string of prayer beads, still warm.
Something below the water is breathing in time with you.

choices.text: Lower the lantern into the well
Take the beads and climb out
Break the seal on Grandmother's letter

premium.teaser: What did the family bury here?

paragraphs: "My child — if you are reading this, it has finally called you home."

"In 1947 your great-grandfather dug this well too deep and struck a cold spring that was never meant for men. A jinni of the water — a qareen who lost its master — rose from it. It cannot lie, but it can borrow. It borrows the voices of the dead we miss the most."

"It has one weakness. It cannot cross a line of remembrance. Wrap the beads about the well-lid, say the names of Allah, and it must sleep. Do not argue with it. Do not ask it anything. A question is an invitation."
The ink on the last line is smeared — as if someone cried. Or as if something had read it first.
You run. The courtyard stretches impossibly long, the gate always one step further than it was.
Behind you, your mother's voice is no longer warm. "Why are you leaving me again?"
The gate is chained from the inside. You do not remember closing it.
A hand — small, wet, cold as river stone — rests on your shoulder.

choices.text: Turn around and look at her
Close your eyes and recite, out loud

paragraphs: The words come slowly, then all at once, rolling out of you like a tide you did not know you carried.
The air in the courtyard changes. Jasmine — real jasmine, living jasmine — floods the dark. The voice shrieks, then drops into a hiss of a hundred voices layered together, none of them your mother's.
The well-lid begins to grind sideways. Cold white fingers curl around its edge.
Far away, the first call of Fajr is still hours off. You must hold until then.

choices.text: Wrap the prayer beads around the well-lid

paragraphs: The lantern light touches the water. For a moment you see only your own reflection — then it smiles, and you did not.
The reflection reaches up. It is so gentle when it takes your wrist.
"Thank you for coming home."
In the morning the village boys find an unlocked taxi-receipt on the cellar steps, and a new name scratched into the brick.

ending.title: Ending: The Name on the Brick

paragraphs: You turn. It has your mother's face, exactly as in the photograph. Almost exactly. The mouth is too wide, and it does not blink.
"There you are," it says, using your voice.
Your mouth is already answering.
Hours pass like years. Your throat bleeds. The hissing never stops, only circles.
Then, from the far mosque, thin and clear over the fields: the call to Fajr.
The well-lid slams shut. The courtyard is empty, grey and quiet. Birds begin to sing as though nothing has happened.
On the cellar steps, written in wet footprints leading up, are the words: SEE YOU TONIGHT.

ending.title: You survived the night — but it is not over.

paragraphs: The beads settle around the stone lid and glow, one by one, like a string of tiny moons.
The thing in the well makes a sound you will hear in every quiet room for the rest of your life — not rage, but grief. Then silence.
The jasmine on the walls blooms white. In the soft grey before Fajr, you hear your real mother's lullaby, very faintly, from very far, before it fades for good.
The well is sealed. For now.
By day the village is kind. Too kind. Every elder you meet looks at your wrists, checking for marks, and then looks away.
At the tea stall an old man presses a small iron key into your hand. "The Imam's house," he whispers. "Before sunset. Tell no one I spoke."

choices.text: Wait and watch the old man
